angles.label: The timing bottleneck nobody mentions
angles.text: Tracing and recovery are sequential, not parallel—you need a forensic map before any legal move makes sense. The difference between 48 hours and 48 days into a freeze window often determines whether assets are still at a centralised exchange or already layered through bridges and mixers.

angles.label: Evidence that actually works in court
angles.text: Raw blockchain data is not evidence. Prosecutors and judges need a narrative: where it came from, how it moved, and where it is now—with every step traceable to a specific transaction and timestamp. Courts reject 'we found it on-chain' without the chain of custody.

angles.label: When tracing hits a hard wall
angles.text: Not every theft is recoverable, even with perfect forensics. Once funds reach a decentralised exchange, a privacy mixer, or an uncooperative jurisdiction, tracing continues but recovery options collapse. The forensic question and the legal question are different.

angles.label: Crypto discovery is not guesswork
angles.text: You cannot find what you do not know to look for. The tracing starts with exchange account identifiers, wallet addresses or transaction hashes—not vague suspicions. A competent forensic assessment tells you whether hidden assets exist and roughly where to search before expensive litigation.

angles.label: The source-of-funds proof lawyers need
angles.text: 'Spouse has a wallet' is not enough for a court. You need evidence of how funds entered that wallet, from what income or assets, and when. Blockchain forensics can trace backwards to the employment, business or settlement source—the narrative courts actually use to rule on division.

angles.label: Speed advantage in family law
angles.text: Unlike criminal cases, divorce timelines are often compressed. Forensic tracing before trial can shift settlement dynamics entirely. The sooner you know what exists and where it is, the sooner your negotiating position hardens.

angles.label: The compliance question exchanges miss
angles.text: 'It came from Coinbase' is not source of funds. You need to trace it backward: where did the user acquire the coins before deposit? Employment, business income, inheritance, or something else? Exchanges that skip this step are licensing risks under MiCA and other regimes.

angles.label: Why timing and jurisdiction matter
angles.text: Source of funds verification is cheapest and cleanest when funds are fresh and transaction history is short. A six-month-old wallet with 50 transfers across five chains costs five times more to verify than a direct bank-to-exchange deposit. Compliance frameworks should incentivise early verification, not late.

angles.label: The mixer problem compliance creates
angles.text: Once a user deposits through a privacy mixer or uses a bridge from an opaque source, the source-of-funds chain breaks. Compliance officers then face a choice: reject the deposit or accept elevated risk. Understanding where that line is in your KYC process is non-negotiable.

angles.label: Forensics is MiCA's blind spot
angles.text: MiCA sets governance and operational standards but is largely silent on ongoing surveillance of wallet activity after deposit. VASP licensing under MiCA requires you to know your customer's source of funds and ongoing transaction risk—forensic data, not just KYC forms. Many compliance teams are still building this muscle.

angles.label: The frozen asset notification gap
angles.text: Under MiCA, VASPs will need to report suspected frozen or disputed assets to supervisors. Knowing whether your customer's withdrawal is delayed due to regulatory freeze, law enforcement hold, or technical issue requires forensic visibility. Having that data ready is a compliance edge.

angles.label: AML filing quality under MiCA pressure
angles.text: MiCA raises scrutiny on VASP AML controls. A suspicious activity report that says 'user transferred to unidentified address' is weak. One that says 'traced to known mixing service used in ransomware cases' is defensible. Forensic precision in AML filings is moving from nice-to-have to regulatory expectation.

angles.label: The data you need but do not collect
angles.text: Most AML teams flag suspicious patterns—velocity, round amounts, routing through mixers—but cannot tell you what came before the user hit your exchange. Blockchain tracing fills that gap: you can now see whether this is a long-established wallet or a fresh one designed to obscure its source. That changes risk scoring completely.

angles.label: Why mixer detection alone is insufficient
angles.text: Yes, you can tag deposits from known mixing services. But not all mixer transactions are illicit, and many illicit funds never touch mixers—they just move through legitimate bridges and swaps. Effective AML on crypto requires tracing intent and source, not just flagging tools.

angles.label: SAR narratives that survive scrutiny
angles.text: A Suspicious Activity Report that names the mixing service, traces the pre-mixer history, and links it to a known scam or ransomware campaign will survive regulator review. One that just says 'unknown risk' will not. Forensic precision in AML filing is how you demonstrate genuine due diligence.

angles.label: The first 72 hours determine everything
angles.text: Within three days of a ransomware hit, you need to know: where did the attacker move the ransom? Is it still in a hot wallet, at an exchange, or already cashed out? Speed determines whether law enforcement can coordinate a freeze or asset recovery. After layering begins, the window closes.

angles.label: Why forensics comes before the negotiator
angles.text: You cannot negotiate ransom credibly or assess payment demands without knowing what the attacker actually controls. Forensic tracing tells you whether they hold your keys, your backups, or just encrypted files. That distinction changes your response strategy entirely.

angles.label: EU coordination requires traceable evidence
angles.text: Under NIS2 and DORA, ransomware incidents must be reported. Cross-border recovery coordination (UK, US, EU) requires forensic evidence that stands up to legal scrutiny in multiple jurisdictions. An incident report backed by a clean tracing timeline moves faster than unverified claims.

angles.label: What 'proof of incident' actually means
angles.text: NIS2 incident reports must include timelines, evidence of compromise, and impact scope. For financial crime or ransomware, this means traceable forensic data: which systems, which accounts, which transactions. Blockchain incidents are blind without tracing—you cannot report confidently without it.

angles.label: The timeline credibility problem
angles.text: Regulators scrutinise when you detected a breach versus when you actually notified. If you say 'we noticed funds were missing', you need to prove via blockchain forensics when they actually left—not when your accounting team noticed. This is where tracing creates defensible timelines.

angles.label: Cross-border incident coordination under NIS2
angles.text: When a NIS2 incident crosses borders (UK, EU, US), regulators expect coordinated response. That requires evidence that speaks to all three jurisdictions. Blockchain forensics, being immutable and global, is that common language. Reports backed by tracing are faster to action.

angles.label: Crypto is DORA's operational risk frontier
angles.text: DORA requires financial entities to map third-party dependencies and operational risks. Crypto integration—exchanges, staking, bridge usage, custody—creates new failure modes. Forensic tracing is how you stress-test that ecosystem: you need to know where assets actually go and how long it takes to recover them under stress.

angles.label: The audit trail DORA auditors now demand
angles.text: DORA compliance reviews now include crypto operational resilience. Auditors ask: if a custodian or exchange failed, could you prove where your assets are and recover them? You need forensic tracing data to answer that credibly. Generic custody attestations are no longer enough.

angles.label: Incident response timelines under DORA pressure
angles.text: DORA obliges firms to recover from operational incidents within defined RTO/RPO windows. For crypto, that means forensic visibility: you must know within hours where frozen or misdirected assets are. Organisations without tracing capability will fail DORA stress tests.

angles.label: Why raw data is not investigation
angles.text: Blockchain has perfect transaction records but no context. Investigation is turning data into narrative: this address belongs to this entity, this transfer happened because of this event, this pattern indicates this intent. Forensic investigation adds the logic that makes data actionable for law enforcement, courts, or compliance.

angles.label: The mixer and bridge trap in investigation
angles.text: Privacy tools obscure identity but not the ledger. When assets cross a mixer or bridge, investigators see the before and after but not the middle. Good forensic investigation maps the likelihood and cost of that crossing—which tools are used, what timing matches, what other metadata corroborates it.

angles.label: Chain-specific expertise matters more than blockchain enthusiasm
angles.text: Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and Tron have radically different transaction models, account structures and traceability. An investigator credible on Bitcoin may miss crucial detail on Tron or Polygon. Serious investigation requires chain-specific forensic knowledge, not generic blockchain understanding.

angles.label: The evidence chain law enforcement needs
angles.text: Police and prosecutors cannot use blockchain data as-is. They need forensic reports that translate transactions into evidence: this address belongs to suspect X (with verification method), funds flowed via this route (with timestamps), they arrived at this exchange (with supporting compliance data). That is forensic investigation; the blockchain is just the foundation.

angles.label: Exchange cooperation is your choke point
angles.text: Law enforcement can trace assets to an exchange address in minutes. But knowing which customer owns that address depends on the exchange's willingness to cooperate and the speed of your legal request. Early forensic tracing shows whether recovery is feasible before you invest investigative resources.

angles.label: Why timing turns solvable cases cold
angles.text: Fraud victims often delay reporting by weeks. By then, funds have moved through bridges, mixers, or multiple exchanges. The same case solved in 48 hours might be unsolvable in 30 days. Law enforcement should prioritise crypto fraud reports by urgency—forensic feasibility, not just case complexity.

angles.label: Počasnost preiskave je največja grožnja
angles.text: Žrtve prevare pogosto čakajo tednos, preden prijavijo. V tem času se sredstva premikajo čez mostove in mešalce. Policija mora dati prednost primerom po hitosti—sredstva, ki jih danes še lahko spremljamo na borzi, jutri ne bodo dostopna.

angles.label: Obveznost banks pri sledenju kriptovalut
angles.text: Banke pod DORA in AML predpisi morajo vedeti, kako se kriptovalute, ki prihajajo od strank, premikajo po blockchinu. Če sredstva niso prioprečena v prvih 48 urah, je sledenje na borzi pogosto edina možnost. Banke brez tega znanja nimajo realne možnosti za povrnitev.

angles.label: Ločnica med segutnjem in povrnkom
angles.text: Sledenje pomeni vedeti, kje so sredstva in kako so se premikala. Povrnka pomeni jih dejansko dobiti nazaj—in ta proces zahteva sodno odredbo, sodelovanje borze in pravno jurisdikcijo. Preiskovalci morajo vedeti, kje je ta meja, preden obljubijo žrtvam upanje.

posts.title: We are seeing digital assets, such as crypto, becoming more common in divorce. And many people assume the family court can't reach them. It can.
posts.author: Alex O'Dwyer Curran
posts.snippet:
We are seeing digital assets, such as crypto, becoming more common in divorce. And many people assume the family court can't reach them. It can.

Plenty of people going through divorce are quietly banking on perceived anonymity. But the duty of full and frank financial disclosure applies to crypto in precisely the same way it applies to a bank account, a pension or a house. Digital assets are not a loophole. They are just another asset the court expects to see.
 
The fact that a a Form E has specific box for cryptocurrency disclosure is no excuse for not disclosing digital assets. Crypto is not anonymous, it's pseudonymous. Transactions sit permanently on a public ledger, and forensic tools can follow the trail back to a person and an exchange account. Non-disclosure of digital assets can have just the same repercussions as conventional non-disclosure as the husband found out to his detriment in Culligan, a case back in the forefront of family law following the recent Court of Appeal judgment (albeit, focusing on "Wells sharing" and fairness, rather than crypto assets and non-disclosure)
 
Approximately 8% of adults in the UK hold some form of crypto, and for founders and finance professionals it can be a serious slice of the marital wealth. My new guide explains what has to be disclosed, how hidden holdings are traced, and what the court can actually do about it.
 
If you suspect part of the picture is missing, it's worth knowing where you stand. (Link in comments.)

Fraud in North Macedonia can involve investment scams, cryptocurrency fraud, fake exchanges, forex and CFD platforms, real estate fraud, international trade fraud, phishing, banking fraud, credit card fraud, romance scams, social media scams, and fraudulent bankruptcy.

Recovery may be possible through criminal proceedings, civil litigation, bank recall procedures, SEC complaints, National Bank complaints, Financial Police reporting, cybercrime complaints, and asset preservation. ⚖️

🔍 Common fraud cases in North Macedonia include:
📈 Investment company fraud
🪙 Cryptocurrency and fake exchange scams
📊 Forex, CFD, and online trading fraud
🏠 Real estate and rental fraud
📦 Prepayment and non-delivery fraud
📧 Phishing and cyber fraud
💳 Banking and credit card fraud
💔 Romance and social media scams
📉 Fraudulent bankruptcy and false accounting

⚖️ Recovery options in North Macedonia may include:
✔️ Criminal complaints with the Ministry of Interior / Police
✔️ Cybercrime Unit reporting for phishing, crypto scams, online fraud, and digital crime
✔️ Prosecution through the Public Prosecutor’s Office
✔️ Financial Police Office involvement for financial crime, money laundering, false accounting, and financial misconduct
✔️ Civil claims before Macedonian courts
✔️ SEC complaints for investment, forex, CFD, capital market, and unauthorised investment activity
✔️ National Bank complaints for banking, payment, and bank-related fraud
✔️ Interim measures, asset attachment, and preservation orders before Macedonian courts

🛡️ Immediate steps after discovering fraud:
🏦 Notify your bank, card issuer, or payment provider immediately
🚔 File a criminal complaint with the Ministry of Interior / Police
💻 Report cyber-enabled fraud to the Cybercrime Unit or Cybercrime Department
📩 Notify the SEC if the fraud involves an investment firm, forex platform, CFD provider, or capital market participant
🏛️ Notify the National Bank if the matter involves a bank, payment service, or unauthorised transaction
📂 Preserve contracts, invoices, emails, screenshots, payment records, wallet data, website captures, and transaction references

🌐 Prepare formal complaints and court filings in Macedonian

⏳ Speed matters. Same-day reporting helps banks, investigators, regulators, and financial crime authorities trace funds before they are moved, layered, or withdrawn.

Fraud recovery in North Macedonia is strongest when criminal, civil, banking, regulatory, cybercrime, financial police, and asset-preservation channels are activated together.

posts.author: Veon Szu Khaw
posts.snippet:
#AMustRead 🔆
🟡"Why digital asset fraud victims won't sue"by Edmund Yong

📌 #Summary
The article details why victims of cryptocurrency/digital asset fraud rarely pursue legal action to recover stolen funds. Through a scenario involving a buyer scammed during a cross-border Bitcoin purchase, the author highlights how the decentralized, cross-border, and anonymous nature of blockchains creates severe jurisdiction, identification, and legal enforcement hurdles that make civil litigation practically ineffective.

💡 #KeyTakeaways
 1. The Jurisdictional Nightmare ("Omni-territorial"):Unlike centralized cloud servers, public blockchains operate on global node networks. Determining #where the crime occurred or #whichcourt has jurisdiction is nearly impossible.

2. Anonymous / Non-Existent Defendants: Victims often face "Persons Unknown" or automated bots (dApps/DAOs) that are not recognized as legal entities that can be sued.

 3. High Obstacles to Legal Discovery:
 3.1 Tracing funds to a crypto exchange (DAX) is often not enough to freeze them quickly.
3.2 Courts rarely grant disclosure orders to compel exchanges to reveal customer names.
3.3 Serving court documents (e.g., via NFT to a wallet address) is tricky and unreliable.
3.4 Low Recovery Rates:
~78% of crypto crimes are never reported to authorities.
~93% of victims do not even report within 24 hours.
~Less than 6% consult a lawyer, and only US1 is recovered for every US65 lost.

4. The Vicious Cycle:Because victims don't sue or report, authorities lack data to create better laws, courts lack cases to set precedents, and fraudsters grow bolder without fear of legal reprisal.

🎯 #ActionableItems
5. Pre-Transaction Due Diligence (Prevention First)
5.1 Get Advice Beforehand: Seek legal/technical advice #before initiating high-value cross-border crypto transactions, not after a loss occurs.
5.2 Verify Counterparties & Interfaces: Ensure you are interacting with a verified, legally accountable entity—not an anonymous wallet, unverified bot, or decentralized app (dApp).

6. Immediate Steps If Fraud Occurs
6.1 Act Within #24Hours: Response time is critical. Immediately track transactions via a blockchain explorer to see where funds are moving.

7. Engage Blockchain Tracing Experts:  Hire experts to trace fund movements quickly before assets are laundered through offshore exchanges or mixers.

8. Report Immediately to Law Enforcement:  Even if recovery seems unlikely, filing a formal report feeds crucial data to law enforcement and cybersecurity agencies to build cases and drive regulatory reform.

posts.title: 𝑰𝒔 𝑫𝑶𝑹𝑨 𝒓𝒆𝒂𝒍𝒍𝒚 𝒂𝒃𝒐𝒖𝒕 𝒄𝒚𝒃𝒆𝒓𝒔𝒆𝒄𝒖𝒓𝒊𝒕𝒚?
posts.author: Alexandra Lobko
posts.snippet:
𝑰𝒔 𝑫𝑶𝑹𝑨 𝒓𝒆𝒂𝒍𝒍𝒚 𝒂𝒃𝒐𝒖𝒕 𝒄𝒚𝒃𝒆𝒓𝒔𝒆𝒄𝒖𝒓𝒊𝒕𝒚? 

That’s the question I found myself asking while reading about the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA). At first, it looked like another regulation focused on cybersecurity. But the more I read, the more I felt that cybersecurity isn’t actually the main message. What if DORA isn’t trying to prevent every cyberattack? What if it’s trying to change the way organizations think about risk?

No system is perfect. Technology fails, people make mistakes, and new threats appear every day. If that’s the reality organizations operate in, then measuring success by whether “nothing went wrong” no longer seems realistic. The more I thought about it, the more I realized that perhaps we’ve been asking the wrong question.
Instead of asking how to eliminate every possible risk, maybe we should be asking something different: Can an organization continue to operate when something does go wrong?

To me, that’s where DORA becomes interesting. I don’t see it as another cybersecurity regulation. I see it as a framework that shifts the focus from prevention to resilience. Preventing incidents will always be important, but DORA seems to recognize something many organizations already know: prevention isn’t always enough. What matters just as much is how quickly an organization can respond, recover, and continue operating when an incident inevitably occurs.

That changes the conversation. Risk management is no longer only about reducing the likelihood of disruption. It’s also about reducing the consequences when disruption happens. In other words, the goal isn’t to create an organization where nothing ever goes wrong. It’s to create one where a single incident doesn’t become a business crisis.

Studying finance and risk management has made me appreciate this shift in perspective. We often evaluate risk management by looking at what was prevented, but perhaps we should also evaluate it by looking at how organizations perform when prevention fails.

This is simply my perspective based on what I’ve read so far. As always, I’d be happy to hear different opinions.

posts.title: An AI agent just ran a cyberattack on the finance ministry. Without a human in the loop.
posts.author: Asaf Levy
posts.snippet:
An AI agent just ran a cyberattack on the finance ministry. Without a human in the loop.

This week, researchers uncovered an operation against Thailand's Ministry of Finance where the attacker deployed Hermes - an open-source AI agent - in what the tool's own documentation calls "YOLO mode." No human approval at any step. The agent did the reconnaissance, found privilege escalation paths, deployed web shells, and tested credentials against internal mail servers. 585 files recovered. Active compromise of government financial infrastructure.

I've seen automated attacks before. This is different.

The speed is different. The consistency is different. And critically - the tool is free, open-source, and anyone can download it today.

DORA came into force in January. The regulation was written with exactly this threat profile in mind: sophisticated, fast, hard to attribute, targeting financial infrastructure. The pillars are clear - ICT risk management, mandatory incident reporting, third-party tool risk, operational resilience testing.

What I'm seeing in most DORA compliance programs is the documentation is there. The policies are filed. The ICT risk register exists.

But the threat model inside that register still assumes a human behind the keyboard.

That assumption is now outdated.

If your SOC detection rules, your incident response playbooks, and your third-party risk assessments were all designed around human-speed attacks - you have a gap. AI agents operate differently. They don't take breaks. They don't make the same mistakes humans do. And they don't show up in your logs the way a person would.

DORA compliance isn't a one-time project. The threat it was designed to address just changed.

Has your ICT risk framework been updated since AI agents became operational weapons?

posts.title: 𝗣𝗖𝗜 𝗗𝗦𝗦 𝘃𝘀 𝗜𝗦𝗢 𝟮𝟳𝟬𝟬𝟭 𝘃𝘀 𝗡𝗜𝗦𝗧 𝘃𝘀 𝗗𝗢𝗥𝗔 — What’s the actual difference?
posts.author: Hadi Khan
posts.snippet:
𝗣𝗖𝗜 𝗗𝗦𝗦 𝘃𝘀 𝗜𝗦𝗢 𝟮𝟳𝟬𝟬𝟭 𝘃𝘀 𝗡𝗜𝗦𝗧 𝘃𝘀 𝗗𝗢𝗥𝗔 — What’s the actual difference?


If you work in IT, cloud, or network security, you’ve heard all four names thrown around like they’re interchangeable. They’re not. Each one exists to solve a different problem, for a different audience.
Here’s a quick breakdown 👇
🔒 𝗣𝗖𝗜 𝗗𝗦𝗦 (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard)
→ Who it’s for: Any business that stores, processes, or transmits cardholder data
→ Focus: Protecting payment card transactions and cardholder data specifically
→ Key points: Secure network architecture, encryption of cardholder data, access control, regular vulnerability scanning, and continuous monitoring/logging
→ Where it’s used: Retail, e-commerce, banking, and any merchant or payment processor globally
🌍 𝗜𝗦𝗢 𝟮𝟳𝟬𝟬𝟭
→ Who it’s for: Any organization wanting a formal, certifiable Information Security Management System (ISMS)
→ Focus: Broad, risk-based approach to managing information security across the whole business — not just one data type
→ Key points: Risk assessment and treatment, defined security policies, asset management, continual improvement (PDCA cycle)
→ Where it’s used: Internationally recognized; common requirement in vendor/client due diligence across every industry
🛡️ 𝗡𝗜𝗦𝗧 (commonly referring to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework)
→ Who it’s for: Primarily US federal agencies and contractors, but adopted voluntarily worldwide
→ Focus: A flexible framework (not a certification) built around five functions — Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
→ Key points: Risk management guidance rather than strict pass/fail controls; highly adaptable to organization size and maturity
→ Where it’s used: US government, critical infrastructure, and widely as a benchmark framework globally
🏦 𝗗𝗢𝗥𝗔 (Digital Operational Resilience Act)
→ Who it’s for: Financial entities and their critical ICT third-party providers operating in the EU
→ Focus: Operational resilience — ensuring the financial sector can withstand, respond to, and recover from ICT-related disruptions

posts.title: In Africa, the most practical crypto story is not about finding the next 100x token.
posts.author: 郑星辰
posts.snippet:
In Africa, the most practical crypto story is not about finding the next 100x token.

It is about an importer trying to complete an ordinary order.

Imagine a Nigerian buyer ordering $10,000 of small appliances from China. The price is agreed on Monday. He has enough naira, but cannot access dollars immediately.

By Friday, the exchange rate has moved again.

His cost is higher, the supplier is still waiting, and both sides begin to doubt the deal. A real order can disappear—not because the product is wrong, but because the payment route is too slow and the currency is too unstable.

This is why stablecoins have a real use case in Africa.

For some traders, USDT or USDC is not simply a crypto asset. It works more like a digital dollar: a temporary store of working capital and, sometimes, a faster way to pay an overseas supplier.

But stablecoins and small speculative tokens are not solving the same problem.

If a market already struggles with inflation and currency volatility, another token with weak liquidity and no real use only adds issuer, liquidity and fraud risk. Without a real payment, trade or consumption scenario, most “small coins” remain speculation.

The stronger opportunity is not to launch another African token. It is to build the infrastructure around real transactions.

A buyer should be able to pay local currency to a licensed provider, complete business verification, convert the funds into a stablecoin and pay a verified supplier. The supplier should receive a clear transaction record and convert the funds through a compliant channel.

The difficult part sits behind the interface: KYC, KYB, source-of-funds checks, local liquidity, exchange rates, transaction monitoring, accounting and dispute resolution.

That is where I see the real business opportunity—cross-border collection, small-value trade settlement, reconciliation and protection of working capital.

Regulation remains the dividing line. Nigeria and South Africa are moving digital-asset activity toward licensing and supervision, but rules and enforcement still differ across African markets.

Stablecoins will not solve Africa’s monetary problems. Wider adoption may even accelerate digital dollarisation and weaken demand for local currencies.

But used carefully, they can reduce friction in real trade.

The best product may be one where the African buyer and Chinese supplier barely notice the blockchain. They only notice that payment is faster, the cost is clearer and the money is safer.

That, in my view, is the real digital-currency opportunity in Africa.

MAJOR DIFFERENCE BETWEEN CDD REVIEW AND EDD REVIEW.

1. CDD Review (Customer Due Diligence)

CDD is the standard, baseline verification process conducted for low-to-medium-risk clients during onboarding and routine monitoring.

Purpose: 
Verify customer identity and understand the nature of the business relationship to establish a baseline risk profile.

Target Audience:
 Standard individual accounts, low-risk retail clients, and routine corporate customers.

Key Steps:

🪙Identity Verification: 

Collecting basic information (Name, DOB, Address, Government ID, Tax ID).
🪙UBO Identification: Identifying Ultimate Beneficial Owners holding 25%+ equity (for business accounts).

🪙Sanctions & PEP Screening:
 Screening against global watchlists for Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs) and sanctions.

🪙Ongoing Monitoring:
 Periodic reviews to keep KYC records up to date.


EDD REVIEW (Enhanced Due Diligence)

EDD is a deeper, highly rigorous review process triggered when a customer presents a high risk of money laundering, financial crime, or reputational impact.

Purpose: 
Gain deep visibility into high-risk entities by thoroughly investigating their funds, wealth sources, and transaction behaviors.

Target Audience: 
Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs), high-net-worth individuals, high-risk sectors (e.g., crypto exchanges, gambling, money transfers), and clients in high-risk jurisdictions.

Key Steps:

🪙Source of Funds & Source of Wealth (SOF / SOW): Collecting detailed documentation (tax returns, bank statements, audited accounts) to verify how wealth was created.

🪙Adverse Media Screening: 
Deep-dive checks for involvement in financial fraud, corruption, or legal proceedings.

🪙Senior Management Approval: 
Requires sign-off from compliance directors or MLROs (Money Laundering Reporting Officers) before onboarding or maintaining the relationship.

🪙Frequent Transaction Audits: Continuous, detailed scrutiny of account transfers compared to baseline expectations.

posts.title: 10 Common Misconceptions About Travel Rule
posts.author: Pawan Chawla
posts.snippet:
10 Common Misconceptions About Travel Rule

Travel Rule is one of the most discussed and most misunderstood requirement in the digital assets space. Below are some of the biggest misconceptions:

1. “Travel Rule is only for cross-border payments.”

Not necessarily.

In reality, Travel Rule requirements can apply to both domestic and cross-border transfers, depending on the jurisdiction and the regulations that have been adopted.

2. “Travel Rule was created for crypto.”

It wasn’t.

The Travel Rule has existed in traditional finance for decades. Regulators later extended similar principles to virtual assets as crypto became mainstream. 

3. “The travel rule information travels on the blockchain.”

It doesn’t.

A blockchain records things like wallet addresses, transaction amounts, and timestamps.

The information required by the Travel Rule—such as details about the sender and recipient—is generally exchanged off-chain between regulated institutions.

4. “Every stablecoin payment is covered by the Travel Rule.”

No.

It depends on who is involved, not just what asset is being transferred.

A transfer between two regulated exchanges is very different from one between two self-custody wallets.

5. “The Travel Rule applies to everyone.”

It doesn’t.

The obligations generally apply to regulated financial institutions and Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs), not simply because someone owns a crypto wallet.


6. “A wallet address tells you who owns it.”

If only it were that simple.

A wallet address identifies an account on a blockchain. It doesn’t automatically identify the person or business behind it.

That’s why identity verification remains such an important part of compliance.


7. “The blockchain solves Travel Rule compliance.”

The blockchain solves value transfer.

The Travel Rule solves an information-sharing problem.

These are two different things.


8. “Travel Rule compliance is the same as KYC.”

They’re related, but they’re not the same.

KYC helps establish who your customer is.

Travel Rule governs what information regulated institutions need to exchange when certain transfers take place.

9. “The Travel Rule is an AML solution.”

Not by itself.

It’s one piece of a much larger compliance framework that also includes sanctions screening, transaction monitoring, fraud detection, suspicious activity reporting, etc.

10. “The Travel Rule is a solved problem.”

This is probably the biggest misconception.

The core idea hasn’t changed: when value moves, certain information should move with it.

What’s changing is how value moves.

Stablecoins, Self-custody wallets., Decentralized finance, AI agents.

Each introduces questions the original framework wasn’t designed to answer.

⸻

Travel Rule isn’t really about moving information.

It’s about preserving trust and accountability as money moves through an increasingly digital world.

#TravelRule #Stablecoins #CrossBorderPayments

For fifteen years, the industry digitized assets. 
The next fifteen will digitize institutions.

That shift is already visible in regulation. 
Early digital asset rules focused on AML, sanctions screening, and registration. 

Those rules treated crypto as an asset class to monitor.

The new frameworks ask a different question. 
Can this organization operate like a financial institution?

Regulators now expect firms to demonstrate:
- Governance and board accountability
- Operational resilience and business continuity
- Capital adequacy
- Consumer protection
- Wind-down planning and ongoing risk management

None of those requirements are unique to digital assets. They define the institutions society trusts with other people's money.

The transaction questions are settled. Blockchains execute fast. 
Tokenization works. The hard problem moved up the stack.

How do institutions preserve governance when assets become programmable?

How do they prove delegated authority, policy compliance, and fiduciary responsibility in systems that run continuously, across jurisdictions, and increasingly through AI automation?

Regulators are not asking firms to abandon institutional governance. They are asking firms to prove it still exists.

Most firms respond by rebuilding the same controls inside every exchange, custodian, and platform. 
That duplication is not the long-term architecture.

Governance belongs in the infrastructure.

That defines the next decade of finance.

Buying crypto looks like one click, but under the hood, it’s a 5-system relay race. Let me break down to you how it actually works:

🧩 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗼𝗻/𝗼𝗳𝗳-𝗿𝗮𝗺𝗽 𝗶𝘀
On-ramp converts fiat into crypto. Off-ramp converts crypto back into fiat.
Behind that single “Buy” button sit at least five separate systems: a payment gateway, a KYC/AML provider, a liquidity source, a banking partner, and a blockchain delivery layer.

🔒 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗾𝘂𝗼𝘁𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝗲𝘆
The moment you hit buy, the provider locks an exchange rate - usually for under two minutes - to protect both sides from price swings before the trade actually executes. That locked quote is a promise, not a transaction. The real money hasn’t moved yet.

🪪 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸𝗽𝗼𝗶𝗻𝘁
Every regulated on/off-ramp runs identity checks before funds move: an ID document, a liveness selfie, sanctions screening. Smaller amounts get lighter review; larger ones get the full package.

💡 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗿𝘆𝗽𝘁𝗼 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺
Once your fiat clears, the provider still has to source the actual asset - from its own pre-funded liquidity, through an API to an exchange, or by routing the order across several market makers for larger trades.

⛓️ 𝗦𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗹𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻𝘀 𝗼𝗻-𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗶𝗻
Only now does the asset actually move - sent to your wallet and confirmed on the blockchain. Confirmation times vary by network: seconds on some chains, a couple of minutes on others.
This is the one step in the whole flow that’s final and irreversible.

📊 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝘁𝘄𝗼 𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹-𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗼𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗮𝗺𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲
The button is one click. Everything behind it - compliance depth, liquidity availability, and which fiat rail you used - decides the actual timeline.
Card payments settle fast but cost more and get flagged as higher-risk by card networks. Bank rails like SEPA, ACH or Faster Payments cost less but settle slower.

One click - five systems quietly negotiating with each other. That’s why two “buy crypto” orders that look identical can take seconds - or hours.

posts.author: Chasing Mavericks

A major milestone for the future of digital assets and capital markets in Kenya.

Tether.io has signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the Nairobi Securities Exchange PLC to explore how blockchain technology, tokenization and digital assets could modernize Kenya’s financial markets and expand investment opportunities for local and diaspora investors.

The collaboration will focus on digital asset education for NSE-listed brokers and retail investor groups, blockchain-based infrastructure for tokenizing securities, fractional access to financial instruments and faster, potentially instant settlement using Distributed Ledger Technology.

Tether.io and the NSE will also explore the tokenization of real-world assets through Tether’s Hadron platform, develop secure onboarding processes aligned with Kenya’s AML and KYC requirements, and assess the potential use of USD₮ as a digital settlement infrastructure layer—where permitted by the applicable regulatory framework.

For the NSE, the partnership supports its 2025–2029 Strategic Plan, which prioritizes technology, greater market participation, operational efficiency and broader access to investment opportunities. For Kenya and the wider African market, it represents an important step toward connecting established financial institutions with practical digital asset infrastructure.

Paolo A., CEO of Tether, described the collaboration as part of the evolution of digital assets from crypto applications into real-world use cases and cross-border institutional finance. Frank Mwiti, CEO of the Nairobi Securities Exchange PLC  highlighted its potential to modernize market infrastructure while maintaining market integrity and regulatory compliance.

Credits to the Nairobi Securities Exchange PLC and its CEO, Frank Mwiti, as well as Tether.io and its CEO, Paolo A., George Mosomi, Arnoud d'Yve de Bavay and the wider Tether team for bringing this collaboration to life.

CEO, SmartClues Technologies LLP | Digital Forensic Investigator | CEH | CHFI

Current Challenges Faced by Law Enforcement

1. Massive Growth in Digital Evidence

Cases now involve multiple devices, cloud data, social media, IoT, and encrypted apps, requiring advanced tools and expertise.

Strong encryption improves privacy but makes lawful evidence extraction more complex.

3. Shortage of Skilled Professionals

Demand for trained forensic experts far exceeds supply, requiring continuous upskilling.

AI, deepfakes, crypto crimes, and dark web activity demand constant technical updates.

Proper acquisition, preservation, and chain of custody are essential for legal admissibility.

Many cases span multiple countries, requiring faster international cooperation.

- Upgrading digital forensic labs with modern tools

posts.title: "Ring... Ring..."
posts.author: Ashley Fairbrother
posts.snippet:
"Ring... Ring..."

"Hello, this is Coinbase Security. Your wallet has been compromised and urgent action is required to secure your cryptoassets."

Recent criminal proceedings reported by the media concerning an alleged cryptocurrency fraud reveal a good example of how complex crypto fraud investigations are often most effective when the private and public sectors work together.

The case involves allegations of a sophisticated fraud targeting cryptocurrency holders and demonstrates the challenges law enforcement faces in investigating increasingly technical financial crime. Whilst the premise of the fraud is deceptively simple, it is highly sophisticated from a psychological perspective, extremely effective, and the technical infrastructure used to facilitate and launder the proceeds is anything but simple.

Before the police investigation commenced, the matter had initially been reported to Report Fraud but did not progress further.

Edmonds Marshall McMahon was instructed by the victim to investigate. Working alongside the outstanding team at iSanctuary, we traced assets on-chain to obtain Norwich Pharmacal and Bankers Trust Orders against cryptocurrency exchanges, before returning to the #HighCourt to obtain similar relief against internet service providers (#ISP). Those enquiries enabled us to identify individuals allegedly connected to the fraud and develop actionable intelligence.

That intelligence was provided to law enforcement, who were able to exercise the powers available to them. As has now been publicly reported, the subsequent investigation has resulted in arrests, asset seizures and ongoing criminal proceedings.

Cases such as this demonstrate that tackling sophisticated crypto-enabled fraud is rarely the responsibility of one organisation or one sector alone.

The private sector has specialist expertise, civil investigative tools and the ability to dedicate time and significant resources to developing intelligence. Law enforcement may not always have the resources, particularly in the early stages of an investigation, but it has the powers to investigate criminality, secure evidence and bring prosecutions.

When those capabilities are combined, victims stand a far greater chance of seeing justice and meaningful outcomes. It is a model that we fully embrace at Edmonds Marshall McMahon to help victims of these awful and ever growing crimes.

Thanks to iSanctuary for their excellent work on this investigation, to the Police officers who progressed the matter once it was referred, and to our dedicated team at EMM, Rhys Evans and Edis Balci.

A 12-week trial was set for Chelmsford Crown Court from 24 May next year,

posts.title: 🚨 Fraud is now the largest property crime in America by dollar value, and most of it never gets investigated.
posts.author: Matthew Hogan, MS
posts.snippet:
🚨 Fraud is now the largest property crime in America by dollar value, and most of it never gets investigated.

That line is not mine. It comes from the new U.S. House Committee on Financial Services report on financial fraud and scams.

Back in April I sat at a table in Washington with seven other officials from local, state, and federal law enforcement. We were asked what is actually breaking. We told them.

Reading the finished report, I can see where those conversations landed. 👇

🔹 State level leadership matters
The report recommends that states build specialized financial crime centers, pointing to the Texas Financial Crimes Intelligence Center as the model. Nearly everyone in that room said some version of the same thing. Federal capacity alone will never reach the volume of victims in our communities.

🔹 Prosecution has to become the priority
The report says it plainly. When someone steals $300,000 from a home, a detective gets assigned. When a criminal organization steals $300,000 from a retired teacher through a romance scam, there is often no investigation and no consequence at all. Until that changes, criminals will keep treating Americans as risk free targets.

🔹 Funding for the people doing the work
The GUARD Act would let state and local agencies pull from existing federal grant programs to retain and train investigators working elder fraud and pig butchering cases. That is real money against real caseloads.

🔹 Reporting is broken and victims know it
More than a dozen federal portals. States and AG offices running their own systems on top of that. Victims give up before they ever file. The report calls for harmonized intake and data collection, which is exactly the gap the Connecticut numbers show.

🔹 Digital assets are the payment rail
$1.78 billion moved to fraudsters through digital assets in 2025. Crypto ATMs sit at the center of it, and Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, US Treasury has already flagged operators feeding banks false compliance information.

🔹 Technology parity
Criminals adopted AI first. The report tells government and industry to catch up, and backs H.R. 8671 and H.R. 5877 to get there.

None of this fixes itself. Reports do not seize assets or lock up bad guys. But when a committee writes down what the ground troops said and turns it into a legislative agenda, that is how the work moves from a conference room into a statute.

To everyone else who sat in those roundtables, industry in December and the regulators in May, thank you. This is what happens when the people closest to the harm get asked the right questions.

Prove the Possible. 🍀

Maritime Cybersecurity Wake-Up Call 

The shipping and logistics sector is facing an unprecedented wave of sophisticated cyber threats. Over the last month alone,  major incidents have redefined the digital risk landscape for global maritime operations:

1. The Adriatic Port Authority Ransomware Crisis

Cause: A highly targeted, sophisticated cyberattack by the Anubis ransomware group.
Effect: Complete exfiltration of highly sensitive emergency plans, employee records, and internal communications, resulting in severe regional logistics disruptions and a $10 million ransom demand.
Solutions: Organizations must deploy advanced behavioral endpoint detection and response (EDR) alongside zero-trust network segmentation (Technical). Equally vital is establishing robust, offline backup governance and immutable data recovery workflows to completely neutralize financial extortion leverage (Non-Technical).

2. APT28’s Rapid Transport & Logistics Espionage

Cause: Russian-linked state-sponsored group APT28 (Fancy Bear) rapidly weaponized a newly disclosed Microsoft security bypass flaw.
Effect: Instant deployment of "BEARDSHELL" backdoors and email-stealing malware, compromising maritime transport agencies across Europe and the UAE within 24 hours of patch release.
Solutions: Implement automated, high-priority patch management systems and continuous threat-hunting feeds to catch zero-day exploits (Technical). Organizations must shift toward strict vendor risk management frameworks and rapid incident-response communication drills to counter state-sponsored agility (Non-Technical).

3. USCG Cyber Command CTIME Intelligence Warning

Warning: The accelerated adoption of AI, dangerous IT-OT convergence, and reliance on unpatched legacy operational systems.
Effect: Critical vulnerabilities across the marine environment, with the USCG noting that even modern AI-driven defense platforms are failing due to weak configurations.
Solutions: Enforce strict Operational Technology (OT) firewalls, legacy device shielding, and rigorous configuration management audits for all AI tools (Technical). Senior leadership must mandate standardized maritime cyber-hygiene training and comprehensive IT-OT alignment strategies across entire fleets (Non-Technical).

The Bottom Line:
The ultimate truth linking these threats is that the maritime industry cannot out-innovate adversaries with tools alone if underlying systemic vulnerabilities are ignored. The industry frequently overlooks two critical, fundamental pillars: ruthless configuration integrity and human-centric security culture. We invest millions in cutting-edge AI defenses, yet allow them to fail due to basic misconfigurations. True resilience requires matching advanced technical safeguards with an unyielding corporate culture of transparency, continuous testing, and proactive cyber hygiene from the boardroom to the cargo deck.

posts.title: When crypto is stolen, the instinct is often to write it off. The funds are gone, the trail is cold, and recovery feels like a long shot.
posts.author: Pinnacle Blocks
posts.snippet:
When crypto is stolen, the instinct is often to write it off. The funds are gone, the trail is cold, and recovery feels like a long shot.

That assumption is usually wrong.

Every transaction on a public blockchain is permanently recorded. Unlike cash or a wire transfer, stolen crypto does not simply vanish. It moves, and every movement is visible to anyone who knows how to read it.

Criminals understand this. They use mixers, chain-hops and layered wallets to break the trail. But those techniques are not invisible. They produce their own patterns, and trained analysts can follow them.

The most important variable is time. The sooner a blockchain forensics investigation begins, the greater the chance of tracking funds before they reach a cooperative exchange or a jurisdiction where recovery becomes much harder. Delay compresses options.

Recovery is never guaranteed. But a digital asset investigation will almost always tell you more than you currently know, including whether recovery has a realistic path and what that path looks like.

EtherHiding: When Blockchain Becomes the Command-and-Control (C2)Infrastructure for Phishing
Cybercriminals are no longer hiding only behind fake websites—they are now hiding inside the blockchain.
A recent cyber threat investigation uncovered the use of EtherHiding, an emerging attack technique where threat actors abuse smart contracts as resilient Command-and-Control (C2) infrastructure for phishing campaigns. Instead of embedding malicious destinations directly into a webpage, the phishing site dynamically retrieves them from a blockchain smart contract, making the campaign significantly more resistant to traditional takedown efforts.
🔍 Investigation Highlights
🌐 Phishing Domain: firelight-fxrp.com
⛓️ Smart Contract (Blockchain C2):
0x967530969F5e5c94E0dC7247e9355e62e0ED65B2
The investigation revealed that the phishing infrastructure relied on a smart contract to store and update configuration data. By modifying the contract rather than the website itself, operators could seamlessly rotate phishing infrastructure while keeping the same social media posts and phishing pages active.
⚡ Why EtherHiding Matters
Unlike conventional phishing campaigns that hardcode malicious URLs into websites, EtherHiding decouples the phishing infrastructure from the phishing page.
Attackers can:
🔹 Store destination data inside a blockchain smart contract.
🔹 Dynamically fetch the active destination from the blockchain.
🔹 Rotate phishing infrastructure instantly by updating the smart contract.
🔹 Continue operations even after phishing domains are identified or blocked.
⛓️ Attack Chain
📱 Compromised Social Media Account

🛡️ Investigative Implications
As blockchain technology becomes an integral component of cyber-enabled crime, investigations must move beyond traditional web forensics.
Modern investigations require:
✅ Smart contract reverse engineering
✅ Blockchain intelligence
✅ On-chain wallet tracing
✅ Website source code & JavaScript analysis
✅ Digital forensics
✅ Collaboration with cryptocurrency exchanges and service providers
EtherHiding is more than a new phishing technique—it represents a shift in cybercrime architecture, where blockchain is exploited not only for moving illicit funds but also for building resilient attack infrastructure. Understanding this evolution is essential for the next generation of cyber investigations.
Techniques such as EtherHiding have increasingly been adopted by sophisticated Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) actors, including groups linked to North Korea, to enhance the resilience and stealth of their cyber operations.

AI GOVERNANCE SERIES · POST 4 OF 7
🚨 DORA: THE EU RULE THAT CAN REACH UK FIRMS THROUGH THE BACK DOOR

The Digital Operational Resilience Act has applied across EU financial services since 17 January 2025.

Many UK firms have filed it under “not us”.

Often, that is correct. But DORA can still reach into a UK operation through its group structure, technology contracts or services supplied to an EU financial entity.

DORA is not an AI regulation. It governs ICT risk and operational resilience.
But AI systems are ICT assets — and AI suppliers are ICT third parties.

That means DORA can wrap around your AI estate without mentioning “AI” once.

🔙 TWO BACK DOORS

🏢 GROUP STRUCTURE

A UK entity within an EU financial group may need to support group-level DORA obligations, including consolidated registers, controls, testing and incident processes.

🔗 ICT SUPPLY CHAIN

A UK provider supplying AI, cloud, software or other ICT services to an EU financial entity should expect DORA requirements to flow into due diligence, audit rights, security obligations, incident support and termination clauses.

DORA rests on five pillars:

→ ICT risk management
→ Major incident reporting
→ Resilience testing
→ ICT third-party risk management
→ Information sharing

⚠️ TWO FEATURES BITE HARDEST

📋 THE REGISTER OF INFORMATION

EU financial entities must maintain a prescribed inventory of their contractual arrangements with ICT third-party service providers.

If your technology supports an EU client, your client will need accurate information from you.

⏱️ INCIDENT REPORTING

For a major ICT-related incident, the reporting timetable is tight:

→ Initial notification: within four hours of classification — and no later than 24 hours after detection

→ Intermediate report: within 72 hours of the initial notification

→ Final report: within one month of the intermediate report

✅ THE ACTION PLAN

1️⃣ Determine your position: EU financial entity, UK group operation, ICT supplier or genuinely outside the DORA chain.

2️⃣ Document that assessment. “We assumed it did not apply” is not a defensible control.

3️⃣ Review contracts with EU financial-sector clients before DORA clauses arrive on their timetable.

4️⃣ Add AI systems and AI suppliers to the same ICT inventory used for operational resilience and third-party risk.

5️⃣ Align incident response, escalation and supplier notification processes to DORA’s reporting clock.

🎯 THE KEY POINT

You do not need to be directly regulated under DORA for DORA to change your contracts, evidence obligations and incident response.

Sometimes regulation reaches you through the client — not the regulator.

AI GOVERNANCE SERIES · POST 5 OF 7
⚠️ NIS2 PROBABLY ISN’T YOUR PROBLEM.

But you should be able to prove why.

Every framework in this series demands attention.

This one mostly requires the opposite: knowing when not to build another compliance programme.

NIS2 is the EU’s expanded cybersecurity directive. It is broad, serious and far-reaching.

But for financial-services firms, much of it is displaced by DORA.

⚖️ The reason: lex specialis

Where a general law and a more specific law overlap, the specific regime takes precedence.

For financial entities:

➡️ NIS2 is the general cybersecurity framework
➡️ DORA is the specific regime governing ICT risk, resilience and incident reporting
➡️ On overlapping matters, DORA applies and NIS2 steps back

In practical terms, if you completed the DORA analysis from the previous post, you have probably already addressed the substance that NIS2 would otherwise cover.

You do not need two regulatory engines running on the same track.

🔍 Where NIS2 can still surface
🏢 Mixed corporate groups

A group may contain non-financial entities — such as technology, digital-services or infrastructure businesses — that fall directly within NIS2 in their own right.

🤝 Third-party suppliers and counterparties

A supplier, partner or counterparty may be NIS2-regulated and push security, notification or assurance requirements into your contracts.

🇬🇧 And do not forget the home fixture

The UK is not bound by NIS2.

However:

➡️ The UK is developing its own cyber and resilience regime
➡️ The FCA’s operational-resilience requirements already apply
➡️ UK firms must continue managing ICT, outsourcing and third-party risk
➡️ Your resources should follow the rules that actually govern your business

✅ THE SOLUTION

1️⃣ Document the carve-out

Record why DORA operates as lex specialis for the financial entity and where NIS2 is displaced.

Do not let the same question be reopened at every audit.

2️⃣ Screen the wider group

Identify any non-financial group entities that may fall within NIS2 directly.

3️⃣ Review contractual flow-down

Check contracts for NIS2-driven obligations imposed by regulated suppliers, partners or counterparties.

4️⃣ Prioritise the UK regime

Direct your cyber investment towards:

➡️ FCA operational resilience
➡️ ICT and third-party risk management
➡️ Incident response and reporting
➡️ The developing UK cyber-resilience framework

The governance skill is not collecting every framework.

It is knowing which framework applies, why it applies — and where your resources should go.

Technology and software companies carry an insurable risk portfolio that's changed significantly in the last five years and the insurance market has reflected that.

Cyber liability and tech E&O premiums have hardened. Coverage terms have tightened. Underwriters are asking for more detailed loss data and more evidence of risk controls before quoting. For risk managers at technology companies, that means the renewal conversation has become more demanding and the data needed to support it more important, at exactly the moment when many risk teams are still tracking claims and incidents manually.

NIS2 adds a layer of complexity that's directly relevant to the insurance picture. Technology companies classified as essential or important entities face mandatory 24-hour incident reporting, board-level accountability, and active supervisory scrutiny. A notified NIS2 incident is also a potential cyber claim event and the data quality of how that incident was recorded and managed will matter both to the regulator and to the insurer.

The firms navigating this most effectively are the ones who've connected the incident record to the claims record so the risk story they tell underwriters is built from the same data that manages their regulatory obligations, not assembled from two separate systems.
